slides.label: Title
slides.notes: Open by separating the two objects students often merge: the surface point is fixed, but the normal vector is allowed to vary along tangent directions. The lecture question is not 'what is curvature?' in the abstract; it is 'what machine turns a tangent direction into the infinitesimal change of the normal?' Preview the sign convention and say that the minus sign makes the sphere have positive principal curvatures with the outward normal.

slides.label: Chapter Route
slides.notes: Use this as the conceptual map. The chapter is a conversion story: a geometric observation, the drifting normal, becomes a linear algebra object, and that object then produces the classical curvature language. Emphasize that each representation should answer the same question, not introduce a new unrelated definition.

slides.label: Normal Derivative
slides.notes: Talk through the image as a measurement device: walk a tiny amount in a tangent direction and compare the old and new normals. Constant normal length forces the derivative perpendicular to the normal, so it lands in the tangent plane. That is what makes the shape operator linear algebra rather than only ambient differentiation.

slides.label: Definition
slides.notes: State the definition slowly and make the domain and codomain explicit. The vector v is used as the direction in which the normal field is differentiated; the output is another tangent vector. Self-adjointness explains why the operator has real eigenvalues and orthogonal principal directions, preparing the ellipse picture.

slides.label: Operator Ellipse
slides.notes: Use this slide to connect calculus to linear algebra. The input circle is all unit tangent directions. Applying S_p to that circle produces an ellipse, just as any symmetric linear map does. The long and short axes mark eigenvectors, while their signed scale factors are the principal curvatures. Trace and determinant then become compact summaries, not arbitrary formulas.

slides.label: Principal Directions
slides.notes: This is the slide where students should see why eigenvectors deserve geometric names. In an arbitrary tangent direction, the normal curvature is a mixture of the two principal values. Along an eigenvector, the shape operator simply stretches or reverses that direction, so the curvature measurement is unmixed. The formula k_1 cos^2(theta)+k_2 sin^2(theta) is best presented as 'linear algebra seen from a rotating unit vector.'

slides.label: Asymptotic Directions
slides.notes: Frame this as a sign test. At a hyperbolic point, one principal curvature bends one way and the other bends the opposite way. Between those directions, there are two directions where the normal curvature measurement is zero. Be careful to say that these are directional measurements; the point still has nonzero Gaussian curvature because the determinant is negative.

slides.label: Fundamental Forms
slides.notes: Use the comparison figure to keep the forms connected. The first form is ordinary tangent-plane measurement. The second inserts the shape operator once, converting bending into a bilinear measurement. The third inserts it twice, corresponding to measurement through the normal map derivative. In a principal frame, all three diagonalize together.

slides.label: Board Exercise
slides.notes: Let students work before showing the skeleton. The operator should feel usable: eigenvalues are visible from the diagonal matrix, mean and Gaussian curvature are trace and determinant summaries, and asymptotic directions come from the quadratic form. Ask what survives a frame change to separate matrix entries from geometric data.

slides.label: Recap
slides.notes: Close by returning to the opening question. The derivative of the normal becomes an operator because constant normal length forces the derivative into the tangent plane. Once that operator is available, the chapter becomes structured linear algebra: eigenvectors, eigenvalues, trace, determinant, and associated quadratic forms.
